cases.presenting_complaint: Persistent low mood, loss of interest in activities, and difficulty concentrating for 3 months
cases.associated: Reduced appetite with 5kg weight loss, early morning awakening, feelings of worthlessness, reduced energy, psychomotor retardation
cases.risk_factors: Family history of depression in mother, recent job loss, social isolation, lack of exercise
cases.mse: Appearance: Unkempt, poor eye contact. Behavior: Psychomotor retardation. Speech: Reduced rate and volume. Mood: 'Hopeless'. Affect: Depressed, restricted. Thought: Negative cognitions about self and future. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Reduced concentration. Insight: Good
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, FBC normal, B12/folate normal. PHQ-9: 18/27 (moderate score). No substance use on urine toxicology
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. Has passive suicidal ideation ('wish I wasn't here') but no active plans or intent. Protective factors: close relationship with sister, religious beliefs
cases.explanation: Major Depressive Disorder requires at least 5 of 9 core symptoms present for ≥2 weeks, including depressed mood or anhedonia. This patient has 7 symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, weight loss, sleep disturbance, psychomotor retardation, fatigue, worthlessness, poor concentration) for 3 months. Moderate severity is indicated by PHQ-9 score 10-14 and functional impairment without psychotic features
cases.management: Biopsychosocial approach: (1) Psychoeducation about depression and treatment options; (2) Initiate SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50mg daily, titrate to 100-200mg); (3) Refer for CBT or IPT; (4) Sleep hygiene advice; (5) Encourage physical activity and social engagement; (6) Monitor for suicidality; (7) Review in 2 weeks; (8) Consider job counseling and social support services

cases.presenting_complaint: Severe low mood, inability to function at work, pervasive guilt, and death wishes for 6 weeks
cases.associated: Complete anhedonia, insomnia with early morning awakening, 8kg weight loss, severe psychomotor retardation, overwhelming guilt about past mistakes, active suicidal ideation with plan
cases.risk_factors: Previous depressive episode 10 years ago, chronic hypertension, recent marital conflict, alcohol use (20 units/week)
cases.mse: Appearance: Disheveled, poor hygiene. Behavior: Marked psychomotor retardation, minimal spontaneous movement. Speech: Monosyllabic, long latency. Mood: 'I'm worthless, better off dead'. Affect: Severely depressed, flat. Thought: Pervasive guilt, self-blame, active suicidal ideation with plan (overdose). Perception: No hallucinations. Cognition: Severely impaired concentration. Insight: Poor
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH 2.8 (normal), LFTs show mild elevation (GGT 78), FBC normal. PHQ-9: 24/27 (severe score). ECG: Normal sinus rhythm
cases.suicide_risk: HIGH RISK. Active suicidal ideation with specific plan (overdose), means available, previous attempt 10 years ago, male sex, social isolation, alcohol use. Requires immediate psychiatric assessment and likely admission
cases.explanation: Major Depressive Disorder - Severe is characterized by all/most of the 9 core symptoms with marked functional impairment. This patient shows 8/9 symptoms with severe intensity and complete inability to function. High suicide risk with active ideation and plan makes this a psychiatric emergency. Alcohol use may be self-medication but also increases impulsivity
cases.management: IMMEDIATE: (1) Urgent psychiatric assessment for voluntary or involuntary admission; (2) Remove access to means; (3) Ensure not left alone; (4) Consider crisis team involvement if refuses admission. INPATIENT: (5) Start antidepressant (SSRI or SNRI); (6) Intensive monitoring for suicide; (7) Daily mental state reviews; (8) Consider ECT if no response to medication or if urgent response needed; (9) Alcohol detoxification if needed; (10) Individual and couple therapy post-stabilization

cases.presenting_complaint: Chronic low mood, poor self-esteem, and fatigue 'for as long as I can remember' - at least 3 years
cases.associated: Poor appetite, low energy, difficulty making decisions, hopelessness, some days worse than others but never completely well, able to work but with reduced productivity
cases.risk_factors: Childhood emotional neglect, chronic stress, perfectionism, no previous treatment sought
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate but appears tired. Behavior: Normal motor activity. Speech: Normal rate, somewhat monotonous. Mood: 'Always down, that's just how I am'. Affect: Dysthymic. Thought: Pessimistic thinking style, poor self-esteem. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Mild difficulties with decision-making. Insight: Partial - views mood as personality trait
cases.investigations: Blood: All normal including TSH, B12, folate. PHQ-9: 11/27 (moderate). HAM-D: 16 (mild-moderate)
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. Chronic passive thoughts ('what's the point') but no active suicidal ideation, no intent or plan. Good protective factors: stable job, long-term relationship
cases.explanation: Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) is characterized by depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years, with at least 2 additional symptoms. This patient has had chronic low mood for 3+ years with appetite, energy, decision-making, and hopelessness symptoms. Unlike Major Depression, symptoms are less severe but more chronic. Patient has internalized this as 'personality' which is common
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation - reframe as treatable condition, not personality; (2) Start SSRI (e.g., fluoxetine 20mg daily) - evidence shows medication effective in dysthymia; (3) Refer for psychotherapy - CBT or psychodynamic therapy for long-term patterns; (4) Encourage behavioral activation and activity scheduling; (5) Address perfectionism and negative schemas; (6) Regular follow-up every 2-4 weeks initially; (7) Consider augmentation if partial response; (8) Long-term maintenance treatment likely needed

cases.diagnosis: Depression secondary to Chronic Medical Illness
cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood, tearfulness, and loss of motivation since being diagnosed with chronic kidney disease 4 months ago
cases.associated: Anhedonia, sleep disturbance, reduced appetite, feelings of being a burden to family, worry about future deterioration, withdrawn from social activities
cases.risk_factors: New diagnosis of CKD Stage 3b, diabetes mellitus type 2, lost independence, financial concerns about treatment costs
cases.mse: Appearance: Well-groomed, looks older than stated age. Behavior: Cooperative but tearful during interview. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Defeated, scared of what's coming'. Affect: Depressed, anxious. Thought: Preoccupation with illness, fear of burden, no suicidal ideation. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good
cases.investigations: Blood: Creatinine 180 μmol/L, eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m² (CKD Stage 3b), HbA1c 7.8%, Hb 108 g/L (mild anemia). PHQ-9: 16/27 (moderate-severe depression). Vitamin D: Low
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. Thoughts of being a burden but no suicidal ideation at present. Monitor closely as medical illness is risk factor for suicide in elderly
cases.explanation: Depression in chronic medical illness is common (affects 20-40% of CKD patients) and represents a response to loss of health, independence, and uncertain future. Requires diagnosis of depression separate from medical illness, though overlap in symptoms (fatigue, appetite) can complicate assessment. Biological factors (anemia, uremia, vitamin D deficiency) may also contribute. Treatment is important as depression worsens medical outcomes and adherence
cases.management: (1) Treat medical contributors: optimize CKD management, correct anemia (consider EPO), vitamin D supplementation; (2) Start antidepressant - SSRI preferred but consider renal dosing (e.g., sertraline 25mg, increase cautiously); (3) Psychotherapy - CBT adapted for chronic illness, focus on adjustment and coping; (4) Liaise with nephrology team for integrated care; (5) Address practical concerns - social work referral for financial support; (6) Peer support groups for CKD patients; (7) Family psychoeducation; (8) Monitor renal function with treatment; (9) Regular review

cases.presenting_complaint: Gradual onset of low mood, fatigue, and reduced motivation over 2 months since starting new heart medication
cases.associated: Lethargy, reduced libido, disturbed sleep, mild anhedonia, no appetite change, no significant guilt or worthlessness
cases.risk_factors: Started propranolol 80mg BD for hypertension and angina 2.5 months ago, no personal or family history of depression
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Behavior: Normal. Speech: Normal rate and tone. Mood: 'Tired and flat'. Affect: Mildly depressed, reactive. Thought: No significant negative cognitions, denies suicidal ideation. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Reports 'foggy' thinking. Insight: Good - wonders if medication related
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH 3.2 (normal), FBC normal, glucose and lipids normal. BP: 128/82 (well controlled). PHQ-9: 9/27 (mild score). Recent echocardiogram normal
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Good social support and insight
cases.explanation: Beta-blockers, particularly lipophilic ones like propranolol, can cross the blood-brain barrier and cause CNS side effects including depression, fatigue, and sexual dysfunction. Temporal relationship (onset 2-2.5 months after starting medication), lack of previous psychiatric history, and relatively mild symptoms support medication-induced depression. Propranolol is well-known for psychiatric side effects compared to more cardioselective beta-blockers
cases.management: (1) Discuss with cardiology/GP about changing beta-blocker - switch to cardioselective agent (bisoprolol, metoprolol) or alternative antihypertensive class if appropriate; (2) Avoid adding antidepressant initially - observe response to medication change; (3) Educate about expected timeline (improvement over 2-4 weeks after switch); (4) If depressive symptoms persist 4 weeks after medication change, reconsider primary depression; (5) Supportive counseling; (6) Activity and sleep hygiene advice; (7) Follow-up in 2-4 weeks; (8) Monitor BP during medication transition

cases.presenting_complaint: Severe low mood, guilt, and morning anxiety, drinking heavily for 2 years with recent escalation
cases.duration: Mood symptoms: 6 months progressively worsening. Alcohol use: 2 years
cases.associated: Drinking 80-100 units/week, morning tremor requiring alcohol, guilt about drinking, job performance decline, relationship breakdown, early morning wakening with severe anxiety, reduced appetite
cases.risk_factors: Alcohol dependence, recent relationship breakdown, work performance issues, father had alcohol problems, social isolation
cases.mse: Appearance: Flushed face, spider naevi, hand tremor. Behavior: Restless, anxious. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Depressed, ashamed'. Affect: Depressed with anxiety. Thought: Guilt about drinking and life circumstances, denies current suicidal ideation but has thought 'everyone better off without me'. Perception: No current hallucinations. Cognition: Concentration difficulties. Insight: Partial - acknowledges drinking problem
cases.investigations: Blood: MCV 104 (raised), GGT 245 (elevated), ALT 89, AST 112 (elevated transaminases, AST:ALT ratio >2 suggests alcohol). AUDIT score: 28/40 (severe dependence). PHQ-9: 18/27
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate-high risk. Male, alcohol dependence, social isolation, relationship breakdown, passive suicidal thoughts. Risk elevated due to alcohol-induced impulsivity
cases.explanation: Distinguishing primary depression from substance-induced depression requires careful history. This patient's depression worsened with escalating alcohol use. Alcohol is a CNS depressant causing direct neurotoxic effects and disrupts neurotransmitter systems. Chronic use leads to depressive symptoms, anxiety (especially withdrawal), and cognitive impairment. Also consider depression may have predated alcohol use. Definitive diagnosis requires observing mood after sustained abstinence (typically 3-4 weeks)
cases.management: (1) IMMEDIATE: Assess withdrawal risk - CIWA-Ar score, likely needs medically supervised detoxification (chlordiazepoxide reducing regimen); (2) Thiamine prophylaxis for Wernicke's; (3) Brief intervention and motivational interviewing; (4) Defer antidepressant decision until 3-4 weeks abstinent (alcohol cessation often improves mood substantially); (5) Refer to addiction services; (6) Consider residential rehab if severe; (7) Naltrexone or acamprosate for relapse prevention; (8) Address social factors - housing, employment; (9) AA or SMART recovery groups; (10) Reassess mood after abstinence period; (11) Monitor suicide risk closely during early abstinence

cases.presenting_complaint: Recurrent winter depression with low mood, increased sleep, and carbohydrate cravings for past 3 winters
cases.duration: Current episode: 6 weeks (started November). Pattern: 3 years
cases.associated: Hypersomnia (sleeping 10-12 hours), increased appetite especially carbohydrates, weight gain (5kg this winter), fatigue, social withdrawal, reduced productivity. Symptoms resolve completely by April-May
cases.risk_factors: Lives in northern latitude, works indoors with minimal sunlight exposure, family history of mood disorder in aunt
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate, appears fatigued. Behavior: Reduced energy noted. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Heavy, want to hibernate'. Affect: Depressed. Thought: No significant negative cognitions beyond frustration at seasonal pattern. Perception: Normal. Cognition: Reduced concentration and motivation. Insight: Excellent - recognizes seasonal pattern
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH, B12, folate, vitamin D all within normal limits. PHQ-9: 14/27 (moderate score). Sleep diary confirms hypersomnia pattern
cases.suicide_risk: Low risk. No suicidal ideation. Good insight and previous successful remissions
cases.explanation: Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) is a subtype of recurrent major depression with seasonal pattern, most commonly fall-onset with spring remission. Diagnosis requires 2+ consecutive years with seasonal pattern and no non-seasonal episodes. Characterized by atypical features: hypersomnia, increased appetite/weight gain, carbohydrate craving, and leaden paralysis (heavy feelings). Hypothesized mechanisms involve circadian rhythm disruption, melatonin dysregulation, and reduced serotonin from decreased sunlight
cases.management: (1) FIRST-LINE: Light therapy - 10,000 lux light box, 30 minutes each morning immediately after waking, typically shows response in 1-2 weeks; (2) Psychoeducation about SAD and circadian rhythms; (3) Maximize natural light exposure - morning walks, bright indoor environment, work near windows; (4) Consider SSRI if insufficient response to light therapy (fluoxetine or sertraline); (5) CBT adapted for SAD; (6) Regular sleep-wake schedule; (7) Exercise program; (8) Prophylactic treatment - consider starting light therapy in October before symptom onset; (9) Vitamin D supplementation (though evidence limited); (10) Monitor annually

cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood, tearfulness, difficulty bonding with baby, intrusive thoughts of harming baby for 5 weeks postpartum
cases.associated: Severe anxiety, intrusive thoughts of dropping or smothering baby, avoidance of being alone with baby, guilt and shame, reduced appetite, sleep difficulty beyond infant care, anhedonia, feels like 'bad mother'
cases.risk_factors: First-time mother, unplanned pregnancy, limited social support (partner works away), previous anxiety disorder, family history of depression, difficult delivery with emergency C-section
cases.mse: Appearance: Tired, tearful throughout interview. Behavior: Anxious, fidgety. Speech: Normal but emotional. Mood: 'Overwhelmed, terrified I'll hurt her'. Affect: Depressed with marked anxiety. Thought: Intrusive ego-dystonic thoughts of harming baby (no intent), guilt about not feeling bonded, 'I'm a terrible mother'. Perception: No hallucinations. Cognition: Concentration impaired. Insight: Good - knows thoughts are wrong, desperately wants help
cases.investigations: EPDS score: 18/30. Blood: Thyroid function normal (checked given postpartum period). Safety assessment: No intent to harm baby, thoughts are intrusive and distressing to her
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Passive suicidal ideation ('baby better without me'), feels hopeless. Infanticide risk: LOW - intrusive thoughts are ego-dystonic, she is distressed by them, no psychosis, no intent. However, requires close monitoring
cases.explanation: Postpartum depression affects 10-15% of mothers, typically onset 4-6 weeks postpartum (distinguish from baby blues which resolve by 2 weeks). Risk factors include personal/family psychiatric history, inadequate social support, life stress, and unplanned pregnancy. Intrusive thoughts of harming baby are common in postpartum depression/OCD and are ego-dystonic (distressing, no intent) unlike psychotic postpartum disorders where delusions may drive infanticide. Critical to distinguish from postpartum psychosis (rare, onset 2-4 weeks, includes hallucinations/delusions, high infanticide risk)
cases.management: (1) URGENT: Comprehensive risk assessment for both suicide and infanticide; (2) Ensure baby safety - never leave mother alone with baby until stable, involve partner/family; (3) Screen for psychosis (critical as postpartum psychosis is psychiatric emergency); (4) Start SSRI (sertraline preferred - low breast milk transfer) (5) Consider mother-baby psychiatric unit if available and severe; (6) Health visitor/community psychiatric nurse close monitoring; (7) Psychoeducation about postpartum depression and intrusive thoughts; (8) Address social support - can partner take leave? Extended family? Mother-baby groups; (9) CBT or IPT; (10) Bonding exercises with support; (11) Review every few days initially; (12) Thyroid recheck at 6 months (postpartum thyroiditis can present similarly)

cases.diagnosis: Depression in Elderly with Somatic Symptoms
cases.presenting_complaint: Multiple physical complaints including headaches, body aches, and fatigue for 4 months, denies feeling sad
cases.associated: Presents primarily with somatic concerns (pain, fatigue), weight loss, sleep disturbance, loss of interest in grandchildren and hobbies, psychomotor retardation, denies low mood ('I'm not depressed, I'm just ill'), memory complaints
cases.risk_factors: Widowed 1 year ago, lives alone, reduced social contact, multiple medical comorbidities (osteoarthritis, hypertension), polypharmacy
cases.mse: Appearance: Well-dressed but looks frail. Behavior: Psychomotor retardation. Speech: Slow. Mood: 'I'm not sad, just tired and in pain'. Affect: Flat, restricted. Thought: Preoccupation with somatic symptoms, pessimistic. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Subjective memory complaints, objective testing shows normal cognition for age. Insight: Poor - does not recognize depression
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12/folate normal, FBC shows mild anemia of chronic disease. CT head: Age-related atrophy, no acute pathology. Pain investigations have been unremarkable. Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15): 11/15
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Elderly widow living alone with multiple risk factors. Denies suicidal ideation but should be monitored as elderly males have high completion rates when attempts made
cases.explanation: Depression in elderly often presents with somatic symptoms and denial of low mood ('depression without sadness'). This is more common in older adults due to cohort effects (stigma), cognitive changes, and overlap with medical comorbidities. Psychomotor retardation and cognitive complaints ('pseudodementia') are also more prominent. Bereavement is major risk factor. Differential includes: genuine medical illness, dementia with depression, pseudodementia (reversible cognitive impairment from depression)
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation - explain depression can cause physical symptoms; use terms like 'stress' or 'strain' if 'depression' is stigmatizing; (2) Medical optimization - treat anemia, review polypharmacy for depressogenic medications, optimize pain management; (3) Start antidepressant - SSRI with low drug interactions (sertraline or citalopram, start low dose e.g., 25mg); (4) Caution with TCA in elderly (falls, cardiac effects); (5) Bereavement counseling; (6) Encourage social engagement - day centers, befriending services; (7) Occupational therapy for activity scheduling; (8) Monitor cognition - should improve with depression treatment; (9) Falls risk assessment; (10) Regular follow-up, consider community psychiatric nurse; (11) Family involvement

cases.diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder with Mixed Anxiety Features
cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood with constant worry, panic attacks, and feeling 'on edge' for 3 months
cases.associated: Prominent anxiety symptoms alongside depression: excessive worry, panic attacks (3-4 per week), restlessness, muscle tension, irritability. Depressive symptoms: anhedonia, fatigue, poor concentration, feelings of hopelessness, sleep disturbance (initial insomnia from worry, early morning wakening from depression)
cases.risk_factors: Previous depressive episode 8 years ago, workplace stress (bullying manager), perfectionism, family history of anxiety in sister
cases.mse: Appearance: Well-groomed but anxious demeanor. Behavior: Restless, fidgety hands. Speech: Normal rate, slightly pressured. Mood: 'Terrible, can't relax, everything feels hopeless'. Affect: Depressed with prominent anxiety. Thought: Excessive worry about work, health, finances; catastrophizing; feels trapped. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Poor concentration, indecisiveness. Insight: Good
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, random glucose normal. GAD-7: 16/21 (severe score). PHQ-9: 17/27 (moderate-severe score). ECG: Sinus tachycardia
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Has fleeting suicidal thoughts when symptoms overwhelming but no plan. Anxiety may be protective (fear of death) or risk (agitation, impulsivity). Requires monitoring
cases.explanation: Comorbid anxiety and depression is extremely common (45-50% of depressed patients have significant anxiety). Mixed anxiety-depression features prominent symptoms of both disorders with neither clearly predominant. Worse prognosis than pure depression: slower treatment response, higher relapse rates, greater functional impairment. Important to treat both components. Differential includes: GAD with comorbid MDD, Panic Disorder with comorbid MDD, or Mixed Anxiety-Depressive Disorder (if below threshold for either separately)
cases.management: (1) Psychoeducation about anxiety-depression comorbidity; (2) SSRI or SNRI (first-line for both conditions) - e.g., escitalopram 10-20mg or venlafaxine XR 75-225mg; (3) CBT addressing both anxiety and depression - challenge catastrophic thinking, behavioral activation, exposure for panic; (4) Avoid long term benzodiazepines (dependence risk); (5) Propranolol 10-40mg PRN for panic symptoms if needed acutely; (6) Relaxation training, mindfulness, breathing exercises; (7) Address workplace stress - consider occupational health referral, HR involvement for bullying; (8) Sleep hygiene; (9) Exercise program (evidence for both anxiety and depression); (10) Monitor closely - weekly initially; (11) May need higher SSRI doses or augmentation (e.g., add mirtazapine or pregabalin) if partial response; (12) Long-term maintenance treatment given previous episode
